description: Mission Impastable is a two-person team of Data Engineering students from Vietnam. We're joining Field Shift to explore how NASA Earth observation data, soil information, and crop characteristics can support smarter crop rotation decisions. Our interests include Python, data pipelines, analytics, visualization, and web development. We're excited to learn, collaborate, and turn messy data into useful insights - one pasta at a time! 🍝
summary:
RiceShift is an experimental agricultural decision-support web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Focusing on a pilot area in An Giang, Vietnam, it helps users compare continuing rice cultivation with rotating from rice to sesame.

RiceShift uses NASA POWER daily climate data from 2006–2025 to construct historical seasonal rainfall scenarios. Users provide information about drainage, irrigation, salinity, crop calendars, and farming priorities. An explainable Decision Engine combines these inputs with rainfall variation and dry-day frequency to generate experimental preference scores, warnings, and transparent explanations. Temperature and hot-day indicators provide additional context without unsupported numerical penalties.

The bilingual, accessible interface helps users explore climate information and understand trade-offs. RiceShift does not forecast weather or predict yields; it offers preliminary screening to support informed discussions with local agricultural advisers.
details:
Project Overview

RiceShift is a bilingual, explainable agricultural decision-support prototype addressing the challenge “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.”

The project focuses on an An Giang pilot area in Vietnam and compares two next-season cropping options: Rice → Rice and Rice → Sesame.

How It Works

1. Historical NASA climate processing

We process NASA POWER daily rainfall and temperature records from 2006 to 2025. The climate pipeline aggregates observations into growing seasons and selects complete historical seasons closest to the P50 (typical rainfall) and P25 (lower rainfall) percentiles.

The resulting scenarios are historical analogs, not weather forecasts.

2. Farmer-provided conditions

Users describe their drainage, irrigation availability, salinity information, soil pH, planting-calendar verification, and priorities.

3. Explainable Decision Engine

A Python-based experimental scoring system combines climate-related water-pressure indicators with crop-rotation diversity and continuity of farming practices.

The water component responds to rainfall deficit magnitude and the frequency of days with rainfall below 1 mm. Temperature and hot-day counts are displayed as independent risk indicators, without unsupported numerical crop-damage penalties.

The system identifies missing inputs, explains its reasoning, and may withhold a ranking when there is insufficient information.

4. Accessible web interface

RiceShift provides six interactive sections covering farm conditions, NASA climate, crop comparisons, explanations, and methodology. The interface supports Vietnamese and English, adjustable text sizes, and responsive navigation.

Innovation

RiceShift's contribution is not a new weather-prediction model. It is an accessible, transparent bridge between historical NASA climate information and preliminary farm-level decision discussions.

Instead of presenting a black-box recommendation, it makes data sources, experimental assumptions, scoring components, warnings, and unresolved questions visible to users.

Potential Impact

RiceShift could help farmers, agricultural students, and local advisers explore how historical climate conditions interact with cultivation constraints and farming priorities.

Its approach could be extended through collaboration with local agronomists, field measurements, additional crops, and validated crop-response models.

Technology

Python, Flask, Jinja2, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, pandas, NumPy, NASA POWER data, GitHub, and Render.

Limitations

RiceShift is an experimental research prototype. Its numerical weights and crop-response assumptions have not been calibrated using local field-trial outcomes. It does not predict yield, profitability, future weather, or actual irrigation requirements.

Historical NASA POWER gridded data cannot establish conditions at an individual field. Local validation is necessary before practical agricultural decisions.

Project Links

Live application: https://riceshift.onrender.com/

Source code: https://github.com/vuhoaii/agrishift-360
